note: Shared expectation table for repository-identity parsing. Read by the Python suite (tests/test_repositories.py) and by the console's slug parser tests, so the two sides are pinned to agree rather than agreeing by coincidence. Written from the documented rules, never dumped from either implementation - an expectation generated from the code under test only proves the code equals itself.
platformHostsNote: Host -> platform, the ONE mapping. Core asserts PLATFORM_HOSTS equals this, the wiki platform catalogue builds each card's hosts from PLATFORM_HOSTS, and the console builds its test catalogue from this block - so a host added in one place cannot go missing in another. Match is exact host or dot-subdomain; anything unlisted is "git".

contract.slug: host[/namespace...]/owner/repo - the canonical identity and the store key. Lossless: parsing a slug and re-composing it round-trips.
contract.host: The DNS host: the FIRST segment, lowercased. This is what a host-scoped credential is shared by, so it is never widened to include a namespace.
contract.namespace: Intermediate segments between the host and owner/repo. Non-empty only for a nested group (a GitLab subgroup). Preserved so the slug round-trips; dropping it would silently re-key a project onto a different slug.
contract.owner: The last-but-one segment. Case preserved - path case is significant on some forges.
contract.repo: The last segment, with a trailing .git stripped. Case preserved.
contract.parsed: null when the input cannot name a repository (no host, or fewer than three segments). Such an input is not a registry identity; a tolerant reader degrades to 'unknown repository' rather than guessing.
contract.platform: The forge the host implies. EXACT host or dot-subdomain match only (myorg.visualstudio.com is azure); never a substring, and never a guess from a 'git.' prefix. An unrecognised host is "git" - a persisted platform is rendered to users, so a wrong guess is a lie that sticks.

cases.note: A pasted remote often carries both a .git suffix and a trailing slash; both must normalize away or the same repo registers twice.
Host lowercased, owner and repo case PRESERVED. Lowercasing the path would re-key every stored credential and project slug.
The port and the user belong to the transport, not the identity - the same repository cloned over https must produce the same slug.
The user half of an scp remote is optional; a colon in the first segment is what marks the authority.

THE divergence case. Owner/repo are the LAST TWO segments (so the repo is 'beacon', not 'platform'), the host stays the bare DNS host, and the intermediate group is preserved in the slug. A first-two-segments read yields 'gitlab.com/acme/platform' and loses the repository entirely.
A slug and the URL it came from must parse identically - the slug is what is stored, so a mismatch would make a stored row unfindable.
A legacy two-segment wiki slug. Still readable as a wiki project, but NOT a repository identity: with no host it can neither compose a clone URL nor resolve a host-scoped credential.

One token names no repository. The api's RepoIdentity reads it as a repo NAME and the wiki's CredentialScope reads it as a bare HOST - both correct for their own domain, which is exactly why the shared grammar refuses to pick one.
A bare host is a valid credential scope but not a repository.
A copy-pasted remote routinely arrives padded.
A second host maps to the same platform - the mapping is host-keyed, not one host per platform.
Legacy Azure DevOps puts the organisation in a subdomain, so the match is on the dot-suffix.

THE case a substring heuristic gets wrong. A 'git.' prefix is not evidence of any particular forge - this host could be Gitea, GitLab, Forgejo or plain git. 'git' is the honest answer, and the operator can label it.
